name: Sleipnir
baseline: CasADi 3.8.0 (autodiff and NLP frontend) with Ipopt 3.14.20 and MUMPS 5.8.1
workload: Optimal-control NLP scalability benchmarks (flywheel with 100-5000 samples, cart-pole with 100-300 samples): problem setup time and solve time of Sleipnir's reverse-mode autodiff plus interior-point solver versus CasADi plus Ipopt.
claimed_speedup: Flywheel (ratios derived from page data CSVs): at 1000 samples solve 11.088 ms vs 59.015 ms (about 5.3x) and setup 0.368 ms vs 19.184 ms; at 5000 samples solve 75.124 ms vs 339.385 ms (about 4.5x) and setup 1.961 ms vs 91.157 ms. Cart-pole: setup 2.147 ms vs 194.851 ms at 300 samples, but solve is NOT faster there (2683.45 ms vs 1251.01 ms at 300 samples).
compiler_and_flags: g++ (GCC) 16.2.1 20260810; the root CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to RelWithDebInfo; explicit -O flags are not listed in the benchmark README
tradeoffs: C++23 with Python bindings; pool-allocated expression-node reverse-mode autodiff that records linearity to cache constant derivatives; uses Eigen sparse solvers; the NLP DSL picks the solver from problem structure. It is an AD-plus-NLP-solver stack, not a general tensor autodiff library.
caveats: Compares a full AD plus interior-point stack against CasADi plus Ipopt plus MUMPS, so AD speed alone is not isolated; CasADi uses tuned options (expand=true etc.) while Sleipnir uses defaults. Sleipnir's cart-pole solve times are slower than CasADi from 150 samples up (for example 3065.18 ms vs 973.846 ms at 250 samples; the Sleipnir cart-pole CSV has no 200-sample row), possibly because of different iteration counts. Flags are implied by the RelWithDebInfo default rather than listed, so tier A is borderline. Author's own benchmark; commercial linear solvers could change Ipopt's numbers.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/autodiff?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars, then the Sleipnir benchmarks folder and its CSVs

name: CTranslate2
baseline: PyTorch (OpenNMT-py 3.0.4 on PyTorch 1.13.1), TensorFlow (OpenNMT-tf 2.31.0 on TF 2.11.0), Hugging Face Transformers 4.26.1, Marian 1.11.0, NVIDIA FasterTransformer 5.3 (GPU)
workload: En->De newstest2014 translation with Transformer base models, measured as target tokens generated per second on 4 CPU threads and on one GPU.
claimed_speedup: CPU, OpenNMT-py WMT14 model: 275.8 tok/s (PyTorch fp32) vs 658.8 (CTranslate2 fp32), 860.2 (int8), 1126.2 (int8 + vmap). CPU, OPUS-MT model: Marian 344.5 vs CTranslate2 525.0 (fp32) and 696.1 (int8). GPU, OpenNMT-py model: 1795.2 vs 6634.7 (fp32) and 10990.7 (fp16); fp16 CTranslate2 10990.7 vs FasterTransformer fp16 8592.5.
hardware: CPU: AWS c5.2xlarge with Intel Xeon Platinum 8275CL, 4 threads. GPU: AWS g5.xlarge with NVIDIA A10G (driver 510.47.03), CUDA 11.
tradeoffs: Runs only models converted to its format (OpenNMT, Fairseq, Hugging Face Transformers and others); int8/int16 quantization changes numerics (BLEU is reported alongside); C++ and Python APIs; CPU backends are Intel MKL, oneDNN, OpenBLAS, Ruy and Apple Accelerate selected at runtime.
caveats: README numbers are for CTranslate2 3.6.0 (early 2023) against PyTorch 1.13.1, TF 2.11 and Transformers 4.26.1; the current release is newer and the baselines have moved on, and the README itself warns results hold only for that configuration. Baselines are whole frameworks, not the oneDNN/XNNPACK kernels; CTranslate2 calls oneDNN/MKL for GEMM, so the win comes from runtime-level work (quantization, layer fusion, batch reordering). FasterTransformer is faster in the fp32 GPU row (6979.0 vs 6634.7). Benchmark script is public (tools/benchmark) but compiler flags are not stated.
found_via: WebSearch 'github C++ inference engine ARM CPU faster than XNNPACK benchmark' surfaced it; also listed on github.com/topics/onednn and github.com/topics/gemm (C++)

name: FasterTransformer
baseline: TensorFlow XLA FP16, PyTorch TorchScript FP16, Megatron (GPT)
workload: BERT-base encoder inference at small and large batch size and sequence length, translation decoder/decoding throughput, both on T4 (FP16/INT8), and GPT-89B/175B tensor-parallel generation on 8xA100 versus Megatron.
claimed_speedup: BERT base vs TensorFlow XLA FP16 on T4: about 3x for small batch and sequence length, about 5x for large with Effective FasterTransformer plus INT8-v2. Vs PyTorch TorchScript: 4x to 6x small, about 5x large. Translation vs TensorFlow: FT-Decoder 1.5x-3x, FT-Decoding 4x-18x; vs PyTorch: FT-Decoder 1.2x-3x, FT-Decoding 3.8x-13x. GPT vs Megatron on A100 is shown only as a figure.
hardware: T4 (mclk 5000 MHz, pclk 1590 MHz) with Intel Xeon E5-2670 @ 2.60 GHz; 8xA100-80GB (mclk 1593 MHz, pclk 1410 MHz) with AMD EPYC 7742
tradeoffs: NVIDIA GPUs only (Volta, Turing, Ampere, Hopper for FP8); built on CUDA, cuBLAS and cuBLASLt; TensorFlow, PyTorch and Triton wrappers; the README says development moved to TensorRT-LLM.
caveats: Speedup curves are images (docs/images/*.png) and the README gives only prose ranges; baselines are 2021-era TensorFlow XLA and TorchScript; the 5x numbers combine Effective FasterTransformer with INT8-v2 against FP16 baselines, so precision differs. Benchmark scripts are listed (benchmarks/bert/*.sh, benchmarks/decoding/*.sh) but compiler flags are not stated. Repository is in maintenance-only state.
found_via: Named-candidate check of transformer-inference kernel libraries; raw README fetched, no search query surfaced it

name: ByteTransformer
baseline: PyTorch, TensorFlow, NVIDIA FasterTransformer (with and without remove-padding), DeepSpeed
workload: BERT-base (12 layers, 12 heads, head size 64, fp16 per benchmark/bert_bench.sh) inference time in ms on one A100 for batch sizes 1 and 16 and maximal sequence lengths 64-1024, with average length 0.6 x maximal.
claimed_speedup: Batch 16, sequence 1024: ByteTransformer 24.70 ms vs PyTorch 53.21, TensorFlow 65.94, FasterTransformer 50.28, FasterTransformer with remove padding 45.22, DeepSpeed 59.96. Batch 1, sequence 1024: 3.16 ms vs PyTorch 4.2, FasterTransformer 4.51.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 11.6 and CMake >= 3.13 required; optimization flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA A100 (CPU model not stated; the benchmark script records /proc/cpuinfo)
tradeoffs: BERT-like encoder transformers only; NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 7.0+; Python and C++ APIs with a PyTorch plugin; the padding-free algorithm helps variable-length batches.
caveats: Tier B rests on the README's statement that the work appeared at IEEE IPDPS 2023 (arXiv 2210.03052, not opened); the numbers cited are the README's first-party tables. Wins are not universal: batch 16, sequence 64 gives 2.09 ms vs FasterTransformer with remove padding 1.93 ms, and batch 1, sequence 192 gives 1.36 ms vs FasterTransformer 1.26 ms. Baseline library versions are not listed.
found_via: Named-candidate check of transformer-inference kernel libraries; raw README and benchmark/bert_bench.sh fetched

name: LightSeq
baseline: PyTorch fp16 mixed precision (training and inference); PyTorch QAT for int8 training
workload: Transformer and BERT training (one A100) and inference (eight A100) speedup relative to PyTorch fp16, across batch sizes and sequence lengths.
claimed_speedup: README headline: fp16 training up to 3x vs PyTorch fp16, int8 training up to 5x vs PyTorch QAT, fp16 and int8 inference up to 12x and 15x vs PyTorch fp16. Tables: Transformer inference fp16 6.24x-11.82x and int8 6.19x-14.44x; BERT inference fp16 1.82x-10.60x (only 1.82x at batch 32, length 128); training fp16 1.44x-1.99x (Transformer) and 1.59x-2.12x (BERT).
hardware: NVIDIA A100 (1 GPU for training, 8 GPUs for inference); CPU not stated
tradeoffs: CUDA only; custom fused kernels over cuBLAS, Thrust and CUB; supports Transformer, BERT, GPT2, BART, ViT and others in fp16/int8; int8 needs quantization-aware training; PyPI wheel only supports Python 3.6-3.8 on Linux.
caveats: Repository is archived (read-only since 2025-07-21). The README headline 'up to 3x' training exceeds the largest table value (2.12x). Numbers are first-party tables relative to a PyTorch fp16 baseline of unstated version; the NAACL-HLT 2021 industry paper cited in the README describes the earlier inference library and was not opened. No compiler flags or CPU model.
found_via: Named-candidate check of transformer-inference kernel libraries; raw README fetched

name: Marlin (FP16xINT4 matmul kernel)
baseline: PyTorch FP16 torch.matmul with dense FP16 weights (cuBLAS), as used in bench.py; other popular 4-bit inference kernels (not named in the README text)
workload: FP16 activations times INT4 weights (group size 128) for LLM linear layers; large-matrix runs on an A10 and runtime across all linear layers of popular open models at batch size 16, with GPU clocks locked to base for sustained results.
claimed_speedup: Delivers close to the ideal 4x speedup (3.87x maximum for group size 128) over FP16 weights up to batch sizes of about 16-32 tokens; the README says other 4-bit kernels degrade quickly as batch size grows (shown in images only).
compiler_and_flags: Requires CUDA >= 11.8 nvcc matching torch>=2.0.0; no optimization flags stated
hardware: NVIDIA A10 (bench.py also handles A100); CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Ampere and Ada GPUs only (compute capability >= 8.0, not optimized for Hopper); needs weights quantized to 4 bits (the repo ships a GPTQ example), so accuracy changes; PyTorch binding.
caveats: Speedup is against FP16 weights, so part of it is the memory-bandwidth saving from quantization rather than a faster equivalent kernel. The comparison plots are images; the only textual number is the 3.87x ideal. Competing 4-bit kernels are not named in the README text. The Marlin paper was not opened. Locked-clock sustained benchmarks are on an A10.
found_via: Named-candidate check of GPU quantized-matmul kernels; raw README and bench.py fetched

name: tiny-cuda-nn
workload: Fully fused multi-layer perceptrons 64 and 128 neurons wide on an RTX 3090, generated by benchmarks/bench_ours.cu and benchmarks/bench_tensorflow.py with data/config_oneblob.json.
claimed_speedup: The README text gives no number for the TensorFlow comparison (it is the figure data/readme/fully-fused-vs-tensorflow.png). It separately states JIT fusion gives a 1.5x to 2.5x boost over tiny-cuda-nn's own earlier code path and that Instant NGP gets a 5x speedup by fusing its NeRF ray marcher into one kernel.
stars_or_usage: 4.5k stars; used by Instant NGP and Neural Radiance Caching
tradeoffs: NVIDIA GPUs only; targets small MLPs (fully fused up to 128 neurons wide); JIT fusion can slow very large hash grids (about 20M+ parameters), MLPs wider than 128 neurons and RTX 3000-series or older GPUs; PyTorch bindings get smaller speedups.
caveats: The TensorFlow comparison is a chart with no numbers in the text, against a 2021 TensorFlow 2.5 plus XLA baseline; the benchmark source is named in the README but compiler flags and CPU are not stated. The 1.5x-2.5x and 5x figures are against the library's own earlier path or a non-fused application, not an external baseline. The accompanying real-time neural radiance caching paper was not opened.
found_via: Named-candidate check of GPU neural-network kernel libraries; raw README fetched

name: faster-enhancer.c
baseline: ONNX Runtime fp32 graph of the same FastEnhancer-Medium weights
workload: Streaming 48 kHz speech enhancement with FastEnhancer-Medium, measured as per-frame real-time factor over 5569-frame clips on Apple M2 and Galaxy S23+ cores.
claimed_speedup: Repository description: '3.3x faster than the ONNX Runtime graph, same quality'. README: real-time factor 0.069 on one Apple M2 core (I8MM) and 0.096 on Galaxy S23+ (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2); quality PESQ 3.054 vs 3.060 for the fp32 ONNX graph over 824 VoiceBank-DEMAND utterances.
hardware: Apple M2 (one core) and Samsung Galaxy S23+ (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2)
tradeoffs: One fixed model with W8A8 post-training quantization; six hand-written int8 GEMM kernel tiers (ARM NEON, DOTPROD, I8MM; x86 AVX2, AVX-VNNI, AVX-512 VNNI) chosen at init with no scalar fallback and no heap allocation after startup; draws on ggml, XNNPACK, oneDNN and Arm kernel patterns.
caveats: The 3.3x figure appears in the repository description; the README text shows real-time factors but not the ONNX Runtime timing, which lives in the linked paper (arXiv 2607.25350, not opened). The comparison is int8 against an fp32 graph, so precision differs. The x86 tiers are not timed in the README. A paced real-time callback costs 4.2x more per frame than the racing benchmark. Single-model runtime, not a general kernel library. Compiler flags are not stated.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than oneDNN" OR "outperforms oneDNN" OR "beats oneDNN" github C++ kernels'

name: FeatherCNN
baseline: Caffe2 with Eigen, Caffe with OpenBLAS, Caffe2 with NNPACK, TensorFlow Lite, ARM Compute Library, TVM
workload: End-to-end CNN inference time in ms (VGG-16, GoogleNet, ResNet-50, SqueezeNet, MobileNet, DenseNet-121) on ARM CPUs: Huawei D05 (64 Cortex-A72), iPhone 7, RK3399, Nvidia TX2, Raspberry Pi 3.
claimed_speedup: Huawei D05, best thread count, vs Caffe2+Eigen: VGG-16 12.84x, GoogleNet 4.45x, ResNet-50 2.29x, SqueezeNet 1.25x, MobileNet 2.65x; vs Caffe+OpenBLAS: VGG-16 10.86x, GoogleNet 13.7x, ResNet-50 3.88x, SqueezeNet 1.68x, MobileNet 4.03x, DenseNet-121 3.08x. VGG-16 on iPhone 7: 284 ms (2 threads) vs TensorFlow Lite 905 ms. TX2 VGG-16 at 1 thread: 1325 ms vs Caffe2+NNPACK 5876 ms (about 4.4x, derived from page data).
hardware: Huawei D05 (Hi1616, 2x32 Cortex-A72 @ 2.40 GHz), iPhone 7 (A10 Fusion), Galaxy S8, RK3399, Nvidia TX2, Raspberry Pi 3B
tradeoffs: Loads Caffe models converted to its own .feathermodel format; targets ARM CPUs on iOS, Android and embedded or ARM-server Linux; small library with no external dependencies.
caveats: Eigen is the Caffe2 CPU backend, not the Eigen Tensor module directly. Baselines are 2018-2019 versions (Caffe2+Eigen scales badly at high thread counts, which inflates ratios such as 12.84x); speedups are computed from the best thread count; TVM on RK3399 (1293 ms) beat FeatherCNN at 2 threads (1420 ms); some wiki table cells are blank or unlabeled; compiler flags are not stated. The repository has no root LICENSE file (the README badge links to a missing one) but source headers state BSD 3-Clause, and some code is derived from ncnn.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/inference-engine?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars, then the FeatherCNN wiki Benchmarks page

name: FlashRT
baseline: NVIDIA TensorRT, torch.compile, PyTorch eager, OpenPI reference implementation (numbers copied from NVIDIA Isaac GR00T and Jetson AI Lab pages, not re-measured in one harness)
workload: Vision-language-action model inference (GR00T-N1.6-3B with T=50, Pi0.5 3-view) on Jetson AGX Thor and RTX 5090 using static CUDA Graph capture and hand-written FP8/NVFP4 kernels.
claimed_speedup: GR00T N1.6 on Jetson AGX Thor: 45 ms vs TensorRT 92 ms (2.04x), torch.compile 105 ms (2.33x), PyTorch eager 117 ms (2.60x). On RTX 5090 (2-view): 13.08 ms vs TensorRT 31 ms (2.37x), torch.compile 37 ms (2.83x), eager 58 ms (4.43x). Pi0.5 NVFP4 3-view on Thor: 51.51 ms vs OpenPI reference 714 ms (13.9x).
hardware: Jetson AGX Thor, RTX 5090, RTX 4090 (local baselines), AMD Instinct MI350X
tradeoffs: Model-specific engine (VLA models, some LLMs, video and TTS) with hand-written CUDA/HIP kernels and FP8/NVFP4 quantization; Blackwell and Jetson Thor focus; long first-run initialization (about 6 s on RTX 4090 for groot).
caveats: The benchmark doc itself says to compare only rows with matching model, hardware, view count, step count and harness; baseline rows are third-party published numbers, and FP8/NVFP4 FlashRT is likely compared against higher-precision baselines. Repository is new (2026) and numbers are first-party; no compiler flags or CPU model.

name: CUDA-L2
workload: Half-precision GEMM (HGEMM) kernels for 1,000 fixed (M,N,K) configurations on A100, RTX 3090 and H100, measured in offline and server modes.
claimed_speedup: A100 (F32F16F16F32): offline +22.5% vs torch.matmul, +20.4% vs cuBLAS, +16.9% vs cuBLASLt-heuristic, +12.2% vs cuBLASLt-AutoTuning; server +25.1% / +21.5% / +19.9% / +12.7%. H100: offline +19.8% / +17.5% / +28.8% / +7.0%; server +41.7% / +40.5% / +42.1% / +22.1%.
tradeoffs: Pre-generated kernels per matrix shape and per GPU (the README FAQ says kernels trained on A100 should only be used on A100); the LLM plus reinforcement-learning generator is not released; PyBind11 bindings and evaluation scripts included.
caveats: Plain GEMM against cuBLAS, so it sits closer to the BLAS category than to DL-layer kernels; baseline_in_list is false because cuDNN, oneDNN, XNNPACK and Eigen are not the comparison. README gives average percent gains only; the paper (arXiv 2512.02551) was not opened. Gains are for the released shapes only; compiler flags are not stated.

name: PowerInfer
workload: Single-request LLM token generation with input length 64 on one RTX 4090 (24 GB) using FP16 ReLU models (Falcon(ReLU)-40B, Llama 2 70B, OPT-175B), plus an RTX 2080Ti (11 GB) INT4 run.
claimed_speedup: Outperforms llama.cpp by up to 11.69x on an RTX 4090 (README: up to 11x on Falcon 40B, up to 3x on Llama 2 70B); on an RTX 2080Ti with INT4 models up to 8x on Falcon 40B and 3x on Llama 2 70B. Average 13.20 tokens/s and peak 29.08 tokens/s on the RTX 4090, 18% below an A100.
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB) and RTX 2080Ti (11 GB); CPU model not given in the README
tradeoffs: GPU-CPU hybrid engine that exploits activation sparsity, so it needs ReLU-style sparse model variants (ReLU-fied Falcon and Llama 2, Bamboo, TurboSparse); dense models get no speedup; built on llama.cpp/ggml code and model format; x86-64 with AVX2.
caveats: Comparison uses ReLU-fied models chosen to exploit sparsity; the llama.cpp baseline dates from late 2023; speedup charts are images and the text gives maxima only; the README cites arXiv 2312.12456 (not opened) so peer-review status is not confirmed on pages opened. The repo is derived from llama.cpp but GitHub does not mark it as a fork. Compiler flags are not stated.
found_via: Named-candidate check of llama.cpp competitors; raw README fetched and repo page opened

name: ik_llama.cpp
workload: llama-bench prompt processing (pp512) and token generation (tg128) for Llama-3 8B and 7B models in IQ2_XS and IQ3_S quantization, on AVX2 (Ryzen 7950X, 16 and 4 threads) and ARM NEON (M2-Max, 8 threads).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7950X (AVX2) and Apple M2-Max (ARM NEON)
tradeoffs: Diverged fork: README says it was last synced with upstream in August 2024; only the CPU (AVX2 or better, NEON or better) and CUDA (Turing or newer) backends are fully functional and issues for Vulkan, Metal, ROCm and old GPUs are not accepted; new quantization types (IQ*_K, trellis quants) require GGUFs quantized for this fork.
caveats: The table dates from the mid-2024 iqk work and mainline llama.cpp has improved its IQ-quant kernels since, so the ratios are likely smaller today. The README itself gives no numbers ('in many cases, better performance'). The table also has a 'this repo' column (an earlier state of the fork before the iqk kernels); its second speedup number (1.12x-2.11x) is iqk over that earlier state. Compiler flags are not stated. Fork upstream was originally at github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp, now ggml-org/llama.cpp.
found_via: Named-candidate check of llama.cpp competitors; raw README and github.com/ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp/discussions/8 opened

name: FBGEMM
baseline: Intel MKL FP32 GEMM (via a cited Microsoft paper), caffe2/perfkernels (embedding SpMDM), a prior 64-bit GEMM implementation
workload: Low-precision GEMM, convolution, embedding and sparse operators for server-side inference, as summarized on the FBGEMM wiki page 'Recent feature additions and improvements'.
claimed_speedup: Wiki page: a Microsoft NMT paper found FBGEMM INT8 had 2x throughput vs MKL FP32 at batch size 1 and 1.3x at batch size 32; JIT'ed EmbeddingSpMDM about 2x over caffe2/perfkernels; 64-bit GEMM 10.5 GOps/s vs 3 GOps/s (3.5x) on Xeon Gold 6138 with turbo off; 60x for 3D groupwise convolution vs the fused im2col base implementation; 2x-4x for 90% sparse operations.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6138 (turbo off) for the GEMM number and Xeon D-2191 for the ResNet-50 thread-scaling number; other results state no hardware
stars_or_usage: 1.6k stars; the CPU backend of PyTorch quantized inference
tradeoffs: INT8, FP16 and sparse kernels that need quantization-aware model changes; x86 (AVX2, AVX-512) JIT-generated kernels; separate FBGEMM_GPU and GenAI packages exist in the same repo.
caveats: Most speedups compare reduced precision against FP32 or against older internal code, so accuracy trade-offs apply; the MKL comparison is a third-party paper that the wiki cites and was not opened or re-run here; many wiki claims state no hardware or flags. The MLSys 2021 paper (arXiv 2101.05615) could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked) and may carry stronger peer-reviewed evidence. Baselines are not oneDNN, cuDNN or XNNPACK.
found_via: WebSearch 'github C++ GEMM kernels int8 CPU faster than oneDNN FBGEMM benchmark README' surfaced the FBGEMM paper; wiki page opened

name: ZhiLight
workload: LLM serving with 3.7k-token prompts, measuring QPS, time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT) on AD102 PCIe, A800 and H20 GPUs for models from MiniCPM-2B to DeepSeek-R1.
claimed_speedup: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-GPTQ-INT4 on 4x AD102 PCIe: TTFT mean 1419.74 ms vs vLLM 4796.32 ms and SGLang 3962.99 ms, TPOT mean 30.97 vs 41.54 and 63.22 ms. Qwen1.5-110B-GPTQ-Int4 on 4x AD102: QPS 0.18 vs 0.09 for both vLLM and SGLang, TTFT mean 1671.38 vs 3085.74 ms (vLLM). DeepSeek-R1 AWQ on 8x A800: QPS 0.16 vs vLLM 0.08.
hardware: NVIDIA AD102 PCIe (1, 2 and 4 GPUs), A800 (x4, x8), H20 (x8); CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Targets PCIe-connected GPUs (dual-stream encode and all-reduce overlap, INT8 reduce); supports INT8, FP8, AWQ and GPTQ; OpenAI-compatible server; the repo is C++/CUDA with a Python server layer.
caveats: Results are mixed in the same document: Llama-3.1-8B on 2x AD102 gives ZhiLight QPS 0.4 vs vLLM 0.46 and SGLang 0.84 with higher TTFT (1091.12 vs 915.58 ms); Qwen2-72B on 4x A800 gives SGLang QPS 0.36 vs ZhiLight 0.18; ZhiLight TPOT is worse in several rows (DeepSeek-R1 AWQ 115.97 vs vLLM 109.86 ms; Qwen1.5-110B 39.68 vs 30.34 ms). This is an LLM serving engine rather than a kernel library, baselines are not in the category list, and versions and compiler flags are not stated.
